reasoning: Failure edits were kept intact and take priority. Several edits from the two groups used the same anchor, which makes insertion order ambiguous, so I moved the success edits to distinct, thematically close anchors instead of stacking them. Success edits moved: the verb-direction bullet now follows the truncated-archive bullet in Rule 3. The song-lyric bullet now follows the date+place bullet. The epithet and pronoun-slot bullet now follows the list-of-names bullet. This keeps each edit's source_type and support_count intact. The success 'passage titles' bullet partly overlaps the failure 'weigh the evidence' bullet. I kept both because the success one adds the headcount/tagline/headword cases. The final checklist's strike-clue-words step conflicted with the success rule for a quoted last word of a title ('The Polar Express'). I added an explicit exception there and narrowed the success bullet to the 'this "X"' pattern. Nothing touches the protected SLOW_UPDATE section.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - Write the answer in plain ASCII letters with no diacritics, as trivia answer keys do: 'Vaclav Havel' (not 'Václav Havel'), 'Pele', 'Zurich', 'Bronte'. Do this even when a passage shows the accented form.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content: - 'The energy / light / heat / power / radiation from this is measured/used by <instrument or device>': the 'this' is the SOURCE, so answer with the simple common noun for it ('the Sun'), not a technical phrase built from the passages ('direct solar radiation', 'solar irradiance'). A bare 'this' that stands for a basic natural thing gets the plain basic noun.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content:
- Person clues that describe an office or role held ('being GOP leader', 'senator from Mississippi', 'team captain'): the answer must be someone the passages show actually holding that role (e.g. a page titled 'Trent Lott Gives Up Senate GOP Leader's Post'). A person who merely shares a stock phrase with the clue ('first and foremost'), or who holds a different office today, is wrong. Check the role and place details first, then use the phrase overlap only as a tie-breaker.
- Weigh the evidence, not the volume of passages. (a) Nickname or label clues ('The "Cyclone State"'): trust reference passages that LIST or define the nickname next to an entity (state-nickname lists, almanac pages, 'the state is known as the "Cyclone State"') over sports-team, fan, social-media or product pages that merely reuse the word (Iowa State Cyclones). The listed entity (Kansas) is the answer. (b) When the context is noisy or the archived clue is cut off, the answer is the entity that appears in many passage titles or headlines and in the page that quotes the clue ('Sangria' pages for 'Spanish name for a party drink of red wine & fruit juices'). It is not a different item that shows up once as a side mention ('Agua de Valencia').

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content: - Pronoun-subject clues ('On June 16, 1881 he wrote an explanation of why he would kill Garfield', 'She painted...', 'His middle name was Gamaliel') ask for the PERSON. The poem, letter, book or deed mentioned in the passages is only evidence about him, never the answer. Answer with the person's name as the passages most often write it. For a clue about a middle name or initial, use the 'First M. Last' form ('Warren G. Harding'), not the spelled-out middle name.

edits.target: answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Acronym / initial-letter clues ('The second "S" in LSUS stands for this city', 'the "M" in NASA'): first EXPAND the acronym by finding a passage title or phrase that spells it out (the 'LSU Shreveport' pages -> LSU + Shreveport). Then take the word that sits at the asked position (second S -> Shreveport). Do not answer with the place tied to the first part (LSU -> Baton Rouge) or with the most famous entity in the passages.

## Final check before writing <answer> (apply every time)
1. Strike every word the clue already states, including ordinals and type words, and keep only the remaining head. 'the Denver type of this' -> 'Omelet' (not 'Egg White Denver Omelet'). 'first to bear this title' -> 'Dalai Lama' (not 'third Dalai Lama'). Exception: when a quoted word right after 'this' is the last word of a title ('his book about this "Express"'), give the full title as printed in the passages ('The Polar Express').
2. Company or brand clues: give the brand name alone and drop the industry or legal words the clue supplies ('this satellite radio company' -> 'Sirius', not 'Sirius Satellite Radio'; no 'Inc.', 'Company', 'Corporation').
3. Slot check: does the answer have the type the clue asks for (person for 'he/she', city for 'this city', state for a state nickname)? If it is the work, place or team that the clue merely mentions, switch to the right entity.
4. Output only the bare answer, with no reasoning inside the tags.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Passage TITLES are strong evidence. When there is no verbatim archive answer (or the snippets only repeat the clue), find the entity or headword that recurs across several titles alongside the clue's distinctive details (actor, director, columnist, a headcount, a quoted tagline). Examples: pages titled 'Phone Booth (film)', 'Eight Is Enough', 'Polonium', 'Funny Girl (1968)', or dictionary pages titled 'fume'. Take that recurring entity rather than a word from the clue or from a one-off passage, and give it in the short form the titles use, without 'film', 'series' or 'element' labels.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - Check the DIRECTION and ROLE of the clue's verb when the passages name two parties for the same event ('took control of', 'took over', 'acquired' vs 'handed over', 'relinquished', 'sold'). Answer the party that fits the verb: 'On Dec. 31, 1999 this country took control of the canal' -> 'Panama', not the US that gave it up.

edits.target: Give the bare name ('Ronald Reagan'), not the event, the place or the date.
edits.content: - Song-lyric or quotation clues (a quoted line followed by 'to this color', 'this word', etc.): find the lyric lines repeated in the passages and copy the words that directly continue the quoted text, in full ('...from white' -> 'rosy red', not just 'red'). Do not repeat the quoted part.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content:
- Quoted epithet or tagline with no 'this' ('He's "America's Sherlock Holmes in Sneakers"') asks WHO or WHAT carries that label. Answer with the person, character or thing the passages pair with the tagline (Encyclopedia Brown). Category-style fragments of the form 'YEAR: <descriptor>' ('1968: Starring Barbra Streisand') ask for the work of that year that fits the descriptor. Give only the title (Funny Girl), not the year, the star or the studio.
- Pronoun-slot clues: in 'In 1986 Sarah Ferguson became the Duchess of it' the word 'it' is the blank. Answer only the missing word ('York'), not 'Duchess of York'.

edits.target: use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content:
- Bare-definition and word-sense clues with no 'this' ('It's the cry of a sheep or goat', 'It can mean to emit vapor or to show irritation') describe one dictionary HEADWORD. Dictionary snippets (Dictionary.com, Merriam-Webster, Free Dictionary) list the senses under the same title word. Answer that headword in base form (infinitive without 'to': 'fume', 'bleat'). Never answer with a word from the definition ('emit', 'vapor') or a synonym that fits only part of it ('baa').
- Form adjectives in the clue such as 'alliterative', 'rhyming', 'palindromic' or 'two-word' are hard filters on the answer, like a letter count. Test candidates against them: 'alliterative bassist' fits 'Stuart Sutcliffe', not 'Stu Sutcliffe' or a nickname.

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - A quoted word that directly follows 'this' and ends the clue ('his book about this "Express"') is the last word of a title. Give the full title with its leading article as the passages print it ('The Polar Express'), because the bare quoted word is not a title. By contrast, 'X is a synthetic type of this material' wants only the bare material ('rubber'), with no 'synthetic'.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content: - 'In <film/show> <actor> played this <descriptor>' asks for the real person or character portrayed, not the actor or the film. Find the passage line that pairs the actor with the role ('Stuart Sutcliffe (Stephen Dorff)') and give the name form the passages repeat. 'This <relation> of <famous person> who wrote <book>' asks for the author, so answer with the person the title is tied to.
